memory_update.text: RSKD should remain a high-priority underfollowed candidate for the consumer_payments_fraud_loyalty node because it is a direct ecommerce fraud and chargeback-management platform rather than a broad payments proxy.

BFH is a second-order consumer infrastructure candidate: potentially valuable as private-label/co-brand credit and loyalty infrastructure, but later layers must heavily penalize deteriorating delinquencies, charge-offs, funding costs, or regulatory fee pressure.
SEZL belongs in speculative_shadow rather than core underfollowed until credit-loss quality, funding durability, merchant growth, and regulatory exposure are verified.
Layer 1B still needs a dedicated sub-search for pure-play chargeback representment, payment orchestration, loyalty-tech, and fraud-data vendors that may be public outside standard US fintech screens.

RSKD is the purest public small-cap candidate for the fraud/chargeback/approval-rate chokepoint; promote only if latest filings confirm improving retention, enterprise merchant wins, and stable chargeback economics.

ACIW is a stronger infrastructure candidate than typical consumer fintech because it has merchant orchestration, fraud management, acquirer connectivity, and broad retail/travel/ticketing exposure inside a mid-cap software company.
PAR belongs in the underfollowed lane as loyalty and guest-data infrastructure for restaurants, convenience/fuel, and retail, but must be separated from lower-quality hardware/POS integration noise.
FLYW is a speculative-shadow candidate for travel/hospitality payment infrastructure; verify whether travel volume and Sertifi hotel-location monetization are material enough before advancing.

For consumer payments/fraud/loyalty, the highest-value chokepoint may be data quality and workflow embedding: fraud models, chargeback workflows, payment routing, loyalty identity graphs, and vertical merchant integrations are harder to replace than generic payment acceptance.

Need a later pass on public chargeback specialists, payment-card component suppliers, private-label credit processors, and consumer-credit infrastructure, with explicit separation between infrastructure economics and credit-loss exposure.

RSKD is the cleanest direct public-market fit for the consumer payments/fraud/chargeback chokepoint; promote to Layer 2 only after verifying chargeback guarantee economics, merchant retention, and fraud-loss assumptions.
FLYW is a second-order vertical-payments candidate for travel and cross-border consumer flows; verify travel vertical contribution and payment-volume sensitivity before assigning bottleneck status.
BFH belongs in a risk-gated alternative-credit/loyalty infrastructure lane; merchant enablement is real, but credit losses, funding costs, and delinquencies are primary falsification variables.
CDLX is a micro-cap speculative exception for loyalty/purchase-intelligence exposure; require evidence of sustainable revenue conversion, partner retention, and balance-sheet stability.

Need a later pass for non-US or recently acquired/private assets in payment orchestration and chargeback management, including Adyen, Nuvei, Chargebacks911, Chargeflow, Kount, NoFraud, Forter, Sift, and Signifyd as private/context anchors.

RSKD should be retained as a pure-play underfollowed candidate for ecommerce fraud, chargeback protection and merchant risk intelligence; promote only if GMV, merchant retention and chargeback expense trends confirm scalable unit economics.

ACIW maps to the payment orchestration and fraud-management chokepoint for retail/travel/restaurant merchants; its underappreciation risk is that the market may treat it as legacy payments software rather than checkout reliability infrastructure.

BFH is a higher-risk alternative-credit infrastructure candidate tied to retailer private-label/co-brand credit and loyalty; later layers must separate merchant-infrastructure value from consumer credit-cycle risk.

CDLX is a speculative micro-cap exception for loyalty and bank-linked commerce data; require survival checks on liquidity, Nasdaq compliance, FI partner durability and revenue stabilization before further promotion.

Need a follow-up search for US-listed payment gateways/orchestration names beyond ACIW and large-cap references, including whether any private chargeback specialists have public parents or meaningful disclosed subsidiaries.

This pass intentionally favors small/mid-cap and underfollowed exposure over mega-cap payment networks. Expanded the universe around scarce consumer-commerce infrastructure rather than consumer-facing brands. This pass deliberately avoids mega-cap payment networks except as implied context; all candidates remain research leads, not recommendations.
